summary: Daily PT ridership has rebounded to pre‑pandemic levels while fuel savings remain substantial despite ultra‑low fuel prices. However, high mobility scores in logistics, construction and retail signal lingering congestion and emissions risk, requiring targeted policy tweaks.

signals.detail: Weekly fuel savings of 35.7 million litres represent 42% of the MCO peak, indicating continued demand‑side efficiency. The ultra‑low RON95 price (RM0.25/L) limits fiscal revenue but preserves consumer purchasing power.

Daily PT trips total 1,494,224, slightly above the pre‑COVID average of ~1.43 million trips, confirming the ridership component of the MF‑Index is at full strength (100/100). This supports a strong modal shift toward public transport.

High‑risk sectors (logistics, construction, retail) show mobility scores of 85‑95 and low WFH adoption, exposing the economy to congestion, higher logistics costs and emission spikes if not mitigated.

WFH uptake varies widely (60% in public/GLCs vs 5% in construction), creating unequal exposure to travel costs. The flat fuel price benefits all users but does not address sectoral disparities in commuting burden.

The MF‑Index at 53 signals a moderate shift away from private car use, reinforced by strong PT ridership. Yet the persistently low fuel price could dampen further modal transition, requiring complementary incentives.

recommendation: Maintain the low fuel price to protect household disposable income, but introduce a targeted PT subsidy that raises daily ridership to 1.6 million trips by end‑2027. Expand WFH incentives for logistics and construction firms to bring sectoral WFH adoption above 30%, and set a fuel‑consumption reduction target of 15% relative to the 2025 baseline.
